articles.title: France braces for another day of mass protests as security on high alert
articles.text:
France braces for another day of mass protests as security on high alert | Protests News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
France braces for a second wave of protests after worst riots in years
By Virginia Pietromarchi
Published On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Paris, France – More than 70,000 police officers and gendarmes are set to be deployed across France as the country braces for a new round of protests against deteriorating school conditions and the rising cost of living.
French authorities have made clear they are determined to prevent Saturday’s demonstrations from descending into the violence that erupted last weekend.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 Macron to meet student groups: Where are France’s protests heading?
list 2 of 4 France to deploy 70,000 police as country braces for weekend protests
list 3 of 4 Are parents in France and Italy liable for damage caused by student protesters?
list 4 of 4 One person killed in suspected ‘Islamophobic’ shooting near Parisend of list
On October 17, protests that had been largely peaceful were marred by widespread looting, vandalism and clashes, with thousands of businesses damaged or ransacked. More than 2,000 people were taken into police custody, according to official figures.
To prevent a repeat, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 20 percent more officers would be deployed than during the previous weekend.
The operation will also involve RAID, an elite police unit usually tasked with counterterrorism and other high-risk interventions. Nunez said its officers would not be directly involved in crowd control but would support other police operations.
Ban on protests
Authorities have also adopted a highly restrictive approach to demonstrations on Saturday. President Emmanuel Macron said requests to protest from trade unions would be examined by local authorities, while demonstrations organised by other groups would be banned wherever possible.
In several cities, including Montpellier, Rouen and Nice, protests were prohibited in their downtown areas. In Lyon, demonstrations have been banned in the city centre, while in Marseille, a union-organised march has been authorised under strict conditions.
Advertisement
In Paris, a coalition of unions is due to lead a march from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes, along the Boulevards des Marechaux, between 1pm and 7pm, after the originally negotiated central route between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Nation was banned.
The ban – and the push of the march to the city’s edge – triggered an uproar.
“This security escalation comes at the expense of our freedoms, seriously endangering the right to demonstrate peacefully and raising fears of a further escalation of violence in our country,” said Amnesty International France.
In central Paris, businesses were shuttered and shop windows covered with protective panels, while some retailers hired private security. At least 24 metro stations were closed at the request of the police prefecture. Major cultural institutions, including the Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay, also closed for the day, while Art Basel Paris cancelled its weekend programme.
On Friday, Macron met representatives of the student movement for the first time since the protests began. He promised more teachers and a deep overhaul of Parcoursup, the admission system to access universities. But the meeting failed to defuse tensions, with student representatives calling for further mobilisation until the government presents concrete actions.
Wider discontent
The protests began in mid-September, when high school students blockaded their schools over what they described as deteriorating conditions, including dilapidated buildings and teacher shortages, as well as what they see as an unfair system for accessing higher education.
The movement has since become a focal point for wider discontent over the cost of living, inequality and Macron’s presidency.
On October 17, more than half a million people took to the streets, following calls from student organisations and remnants of the Yellow Vest movement.
The unrest comes as France approaches a pivotal presidential election in six months. Macron, who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, will leave office in 2027.
The violence has also put a renewed focus on the far right, whose leading figure, Marine Le Pen, has long campaigned on a promise to restore law and order. Recent polls have placed her as the leading contender for the presidency by a wide margin.
Tensions are also expected in Orleans, where Le Pen’s National Rally is holding its party congress on Saturday, marking the start of its presidential campaign.
Authorities expect between 20,000 and 30,000 people to join a counter-demonstration against the far-right party, prompting a major security operation.

articles.title: Czech Republic advances media funding overhaul despite criticism
articles.text:
Czech Republic advances media funding overhaul despite criticism | Freedom of the Press News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A woman walks past placards hanging on a building of Czech Radio as employees of public broadcasters strike in protest at the government's planned overhaul of public media funding, in Prague, June 22 [David W Cerny/Reuters]
By Reuters
Published On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
The Czech Republic’s governing coalition has advanced changes to the funding of public media, despite criticism that it could weaken broadcaster independence.
In a rare overnight vote in the early hours of Saturday, the coalition voted to send the bill to committees for further discussion.
Recommended Stories list of 2 items
list 1 of 2 ‘Orban constantly vetoes’: Europe braces for Hungary election
list 2 of 2 Czech public media staff strike, citing government threat to independenceend of list
The changes include scrapping the 205 crown ($9.45) household broadcasting fee, and replacing it with funding from the state budget.
The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD party, has frequently criticised public and private media coverage of its policies and accused some outlets of bias.
Babis promised to scrap the broadcasting fee before taking office last December, and says his three-party government is now fulfilling that pledge to voters.
Public media employees staged a strike against the move in June, saying it would make broadcasters vulnerable to government pressure.
Opposition parties have compared the changes with reforms under neighbouring Hungary’s former Prime Minister, Viktor Orban.
Babis has said the new funding model would be fairer to poorer households and encourage outlets to become more efficient.
“There is no war for independent media,” Babis said on Facebook late on Friday. “There is no fight for democracy and no nationalisation of media is being prepared.”
The proposal would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15 percent and keep nominal funding unchanged for several years.
Public media are among the most trusted news sources in the Czech Republic, with Czech Television the most-watched broadcaster across several age groups.
Advertisement
A civic group has called a public protest for Sunday, while journalists and other employees at the broadcasters announced a strike for November 3.

articles.title: German police detain suspect after fire engulfs Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest
articles.text:
German police detain suspect after fire engulfs Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest | Police News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Video grab taken from the webcam of the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, formerly Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, on early October 24, 2026, after a large fire broke out at the site in the southern German state of Bavaria [AFP]
By Caolán Magee and AFP
Published On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
German police have detained a suspect after a fire engulfed the Eagle’s Nest, Adolf Hitler’s notorious Nazi-era mountain retreat in Bavaria, prompting an overnight emergency operation involving about 200 firefighters.
No injuries were reported at the building, known locally as the Kehlsteinhaus. Police said investigators were examining whether a “suspicious person” taken into temporary custody was connected to the blaze.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Lebanese sceptical Israeli polls will bring change, end occupation of south
list 2 of 3 Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
list 3 of 3 How Benjamin Netanyahu reshaped Israel’s institutionsend of list
The fire alarm was triggered by a smoke detector at about 9:50pm (19:50 GMT) on Friday. Emergency crews could see flames rising above the building as they approached and found it “completely ablaze”, according to police.
The retreat’s remote Alpine location, at an altitude of more than 1,800 metres (about 6,000 feet), complicated efforts to extinguish the fire, police spokesperson Lisa Maier said.
While authorities have not announced a cause, German media reported that investigators suspected arson.
The newspaper Bild said emergency responders had encountered a motorcyclist travelling towards them on their way to the scene and that he was subsequently detained. His possible involvement remained under investigation.
Maier said inquiries were continuing, with police planning a news conference later on Saturday.
Built between 1937 and 1938, the stone-and-granite retreat stands on the Kehlstein mountain above Obersalzberg, near Berchtesgaden in southern Germany.
Designed as a monument to Hitler’s rule and a setting for receiving foreign diplomats, it offers sweeping views across the Bavarian Alps. Hitler himself visited the resort.
Advertisement
The site, which remains part of the legacy of Nazi Germany, survived World War II undamaged. It has operated as a restaurant since 1952 and also houses an exhibition examining its Nazi history.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro debate policy proposals before run-off
articles.text:
Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro debate policy proposals before run-off | Elections News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Presidential candidates Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva appear before their debate on October 23, 2026, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil [Buda Mendes/Getty Images]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and AP
Published On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro have focused on policy proposals in the final debate before their presidential run-off.
The candidates questioned each other on Friday, two days before the election, about Brazil’s economy, infrastructure and regional development.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Why social media has become an election issue in Brazil’s presidential race
list 2 of 3 Brazil’s Bolsonaro challenges Lula to expand release of personal records
list 3 of 3 What to know as Brazil prepares for tense presidential run-offend of list
Lula challenged his rival’s plan to take a “chainsaw” to public spending in a manner similar to that of Argentina’s libertarian president, Javier Milei.
“I’ll have the same job here [as Milei in Argentina] because you’re leaving the country bankrupt,” Bolsonaro responded.
Bolsonaro, son of former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro, accused the incumbent of allowing organised crime to expand, driving families into debt and not addressing the higher cost of living.
“He doesn’t know what hunger is,” Brazil’s first working-class president said of Bolsonaro, who responded, “Why are things so expensive?”
Lula questioned the senator’s experience, saying, “He doesn’t know Brazil.”
His challenger doubled down on presenting himself as a capable candidate who represented change for the country.
Supporters of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva follow the televised debate between him and Flavio Bolsonaro before the run-off [Juan Barreto/AFP]
Tense moments
Friday’s debate in Rio de Janeiro, which was broadcast on TV Globo, was notably more diplomatic than their initial face-off on Sunday but also saw its share of personal attacks and tense moments.
Bolsonaro called Lula “Nine Fingers”, a pejorative nickname used by many of his supporters that references an accident the Brazilian president suffered during his time as a metalworker. The 80-year-old leader demanded an apology, which Bolsonaro gave him.
Advertisement
Lula in response called Bolsonaro a vigilante, referring to allegations that his rival has ties to paramilitary groups in Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro said he would classify those groups as “narcoterrorists”.
The third tense exchange was between Bolsonaro and the mother of a five-year-old who was killed in a shootout that involved a policeman who had the presidential candidate as his lawyer. Bolsonaro said he doesn’t believe his client was guilty.
Bolsonaro finished first in the initial round of voting on October 4 with 47 percent of the vote to Lula’s 45 percent.
A Datafolha institute survey published on Thursday suggested the pair are now tied with 50 percent support each, compared with Bolsonaro’s four-point lead in polls published two weeks ago.
Both candidates are expected to join supporters in the streets of Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo in their last campaign effort before Sunday’s run-off.

articles.title: Rubio calls on Cubans to partner with CIA ‘to create positive change’
articles.text:
Rubio calls on Cubans to partner with CIA ‘to create positive change’ | Politics News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called on Cubans seeking political change to partner with the CIA, saying 'now is ​the time' [File: Kylie Cooper/AFP]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and Reuters
Published On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA and help force an end to the island’s communist government.
US President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have for months openly hinted at military intervention and permanent presence in Cuba to ramp up economic, political, and legal pressure on the country.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 Cuba forges ahead with renewable energy plans amid US oil blockade
list 2 of 4 Why are Latin American countries building closer ties with Israel?
list 3 of 4 Florida issues arrest warrant for Cuban leader Raul Castro
list 4 of 4 Cuba accuses US of threatening countries ahead of UN embargo voteend of list
On Friday, Rubio seemed to openly confirm this when he wrote on X: “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba – now is the time.”
Rubio commented on “the disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few” in Cuba, encouraging civilians to “seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discreet partnership with the CIA”.
The call was mocked by Cuban officials, including Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio.
“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA… There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste,” he wrote on X.
This is far from the first time Cuba has been threatened with military intervention by US officials.
Last month, Fernandez de Cossio told the US cable television channel C-SPAN’s flagship programme, Washington Journal, that it would be an “ atrocious international crime for the US to use military force against Cuba, which is a peaceful neighbouring country”.
The CIA later uploaded a video on X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official “US embassy in person” if they can safely travel to one.
Advertisement
These latest developments come as a US-imposed oil blockade on Cuba earlier this year has put civilians in the country under intense economic hardship, as they contend with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
United Nations rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as ‌a violation of international law, while rights advocates say the Trump administration’s threats have echoed an imperialist approach.
Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for ⁠more than 60 years, as the Trump administration steps up pressure on Havana following the US military’s capture of Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly ⁠raid in January.

articles.title: North Korea’s Kim Jong Un visits China via newly opened bridge
articles.text:
North Korea’s Kim Jong Un visits China via newly opened bridge | Border Disputes News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
China is an important trading partner for North Korea and its leader Kim Jong Un [File: AFP]
By AFP and Reuters
Published On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge, according to South Korean officials.
The visit on Saturday comes about a week after the bridge linking the two countries was officially opened, 12 years after its completion, deepening economic ties between the Asian giant and its small, nuclear-armed neighbour.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say
list 2 of 4 South Korea to pull more embassy staff from Ukraine after POW row
list 3 of 4 North Korea to resume propaganda broadcasts, South Korea urges dialogue
list 4 of 4 South Korea invites North for military talks over borderend of list
Kim’s visit also comes a day before the anniversary of China joining the 1950–1953 Korean War.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang met Kim in the border city, the Reuters news agency said, quoting a South Korean official.
China’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Kim arrived in Dandong through the New Yalu River Bridge connecting the two countries, the Reuters and AFP news agencies reported, quoting unnamed South Korean government officials. South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency also reported the visit, citing an unidentified government source.
Analysts say the visit represents part of Kim’s increasingly assertive foreign policy, as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War”.
Strengthening ties
Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu River, was a key symbol of strengthening ties between the two countries and reflected their intent to expand trade. It is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks.
Advertisement
The four-lane structure was completed in 2014, but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, according to South Korean news reports.
“The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics,” Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think tank in Shenyang, told Reuters.
“With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further,” Lu said.
China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the reclusive state, although ties have not always been smooth.
China, which fought alongside North Korea in the Korean War, is Pyongyang’s main economic and diplomatic backer. However, North Korea has drawn closer to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which analysts say has reduced Pyongyang’s reliance on Beijing.
Kim’s last known visit to China was in September 2025 to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, where he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June in which he expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

articles.title: Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege
articles.text:
Hospital in Yemen’s Taiz warns of collapse in days because of Houthi siege | Conflict News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Signs of battles between Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis west of Taiz on Wednesday [AFP]
By AbdulHakim Helal
Published On 24 Oct 202624 Oct 2026
Taiz, Yemen – It was approaching 10:30am in the dialysis centre of the Republican Hospital in Taiz when a machine began filtering excess fluids, toxins and salts from the blood of Omar Mukhtar Hammoud.
The 16-year-old suffers from kidney failure and is one of 270 patients who regularly receive dialysis at the centre in the government-held city in southwest Yemen. But with essential medical supplies and fuel running critically low under the renewed Houthi siege, doctors fear they may soon be unable to provide the treatment that keeps their patients alive.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 European, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks
list 2 of 3 US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
list 3 of 3 Saudi Arabia security puts Asian Cup in doubt: Japan football chiefend of list
Dr Essam Mahyoub Dahan, the centre’s director, warned that a complete shutdown could happen within days.
“Because of the siege and the shortage of diesel and medical solutions, we have recently been forced to reduce dialysis sessions from four hours to just two and a half,” Dahan told Al Jazeera. “We know this is not adequate, but we have no choice if we are to keep the centre operating for as long as possible before it shuts down completely.”
Dahan said the centre’s remaining stocks of specialised dialysis solutions were also close to running out.
The supplies, which are expensive, are normally provided by the Yemeni Ministry of Health every three months. But the latest delivery which was due earlier this month  failed to arrive because of the Houthi siege on Taiz city. It began in the first week of October after Houthi advances in the Taiz countryside.
The city was previously under complete Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, in the early years of Yemen’s ongoing war.
Advertisement
Across Taiz governorate, where battles are raging between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iranian-allied Houthi fighters, the number of patients at risk is far greater.
In an October 12 statement, the governorate’s health office warned that the continued siege and obstruction of essential supplies could endanger the lives of 1,110 patients with kidney failure. They depend on dialysis services in the governorate’s hospitals, which collectively provide about 210 dialysis sessions a day.
International humanitarian and health organisations have issued similar warnings about the impact of the siege on the already fragile healthcare system in Taiz.
On Thursday, Amnesty International called on the Houthis to immediately reopen vital roads into and around the city, warning that the closure of the main road between Taiz and the southern port city of Aden threatened hundreds of thousands of civilians with losing access to food, water and healthcare.
Fuel: A lifeline for hospitals
Taiz’s hospitals depend heavily on diesel-powered generators because much of the city’s electricity infrastructure was destroyed during the war that began 11 years ago and has not been restored.
The renewed Houthi siege has severely disrupted the entry of fuel, including the diesel needed to run hospital generators and lifesaving medical equipment.
Dr Shaheed al-Ameri, deputy director-general for technical affairs at the Republican Hospital, said the shortages have had a devastating impact on medical services.
“A very large part of this suffering is because of the shortage of diesel,” he told Al Jazeera. “We have no reserve diesel supplies. Our stocks ran out early in the siege and we are now buying it on the black market almost every day, at prices that have reached five times what they were before the siege.”
Al-Ameri warned that the longer the siege continues, the more prices will rise and the further medical services will deteriorate.
The hospital has already suspended operations in some departments, including essential units, he said.
“If this situation continues much longer, we fear we will reach a complete and comprehensive collapse of healthcare services,” he said.
The shortages are not confined to the Republican Hospital. On October 22, the World Health Organization (WHO) warned that critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicines and medical supplies were threatening lifesaving healthcare throughout  Taiz governorate, with some hospital services already disrupted.
According to the WHO, 42 health facilities in Taiz city had reported severe shortages of essential supplies. Hospitals and ambulances require at least 156,000 litres of fuel a month to continue functioning.
Advertisement
The organisation also warned that diesel shortages threaten to disrupt oxygen production, water pumping, vaccine refrigeration and sanitation services, increasing the risks of disease outbreaks, particularly among displaced families and other vulnerable groups.
The United Nations has separately warned that the restrictions on supplies are bringing Taiz’s health system close to collapse and urged the Houthis to allow humanitarian assistance and essential goods to enter without obstruction.
Oxygen shortages deepen crisis
In its October 12 statement, Taiz’s health office warned that continued restrictions on fuel deliveries could lead to the shutdown of medical oxygen production plants, further endangering patients.
Taysir al-Samei, the health office’s media officer, said that would dramatically worsen the crisis.
“Many medical departments depend on oxygen, particularly operating theatres, inpatient wards, intensive care units and incubators for premature babies,” al-Samei said.
“Most hospitals have already suspended services in some units because of the shortage of diesel and the lack of necessary medical solutions, as well as shortage
